shots.text: Charred grains show what people grew: pearl millet, alongside cowpeas.
shots.credit: Excavation at the Nok site of Ido (cropped) · Louis Champion et al. 2022 · CC BY 4.0

shots.text: Even the iron fits that picture: furnaces seem to have been used only once.
shots.desc: broken clay furnace wall in a trench, slag

shots.text: The team reads that as a sign of travelling specialists, not a central workshop.
shots.desc: footpath winding over hills at dawn

shots.text: As for iron objects, Breunig says everything they recovered fits into one hand.
shots.desc: an open palm dusted with red earth, empty

shots.text: And the sculptures themselves turn up broken.
shots.desc: terracotta-coloured sherds in a pit, unidentifiable shapes

shots.text: Fragments lie in pits, and, as Breunig puts it, the pieces didn't fit together.
shots.credit: Excavation at the Nok site of Ido (cropped) · Louis Champion et al. 2022 · CC BY 4.0

shots.text: The team suspects the figures were broken deliberately before burial.
shots.desc: pit cut in section, layers of soil, low sun

shots.text: Gabriele Franke says they can't prove it, but the pattern is striking.
shots.desc: rain beginning on an excavation tarpaulin

shots.text: At Pangwari, excavated between 2011 and 2014, they found a terracotta deposit in a secure archaeological context for the first time.
shots.desc: generic close-up of a trowel cleaning red soil, no finds visible

shots.text: The team interprets some deposits as graves, marked by upright stones in a row; no human remains survive.
shots.desc: a row of plain upright field stones in grassland at dusk, no finds, no people
